name: Anatoly Karpov
milestone_by_age_26: Became World Chess Champion in 1975 at age 24 when Bobby Fischer defaulted, having already won the World Junior Championship (1969, age 18) and earned the grandmaster title (1970, age 19).
early_history_summary: Karpov learned chess at age four and became a candidate master by eleven. At twelve he was accepted into Mikhail Botvinnik's prestigious chess school, and under Botvinnik's tutelage became the youngest Soviet master in history at fifteen in 1966. He won the World Junior Championship at Stockholm in 1969 at age 18, earned the grandmaster title in 1970, and through a series of Candidates tournament victories became World Chess Champion in 1975 at age 24.
family_context_summary: Karpov was born into a Russian family in Zlatoust in the Urals region. No specific information about parental occupation or financial status was found in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no evidence that parents or close family members were chess players or had relevant domain expertise.
evidence_summary: Karpov's early rise was driven by the Soviet chess pipeline: he learned chess at four, became a candidate master at eleven, and was accepted into Botvinnik's elite chess school at twelve. Botvinnik's sustained coaching transformed his game, making him the youngest Soviet master at fifteen. He later transferred to Leningrad State University to be closer to coach Semyon Furman. By 24 he was World Chess Champion. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources; the dominant early advantage was the elite Soviet chess development system and world-class coaching from Botvinnik and Furman.
starting_point: Born in 1951 in Zlatoust, Urals region, USSR, into a Russian family; father was an engineer.
current_position: Oldest living World Chess Champion; elected Member of the State Duma in Russia; chairs the Commission for Ecological Safety and Environmental Protection of the Civic Chamber of the Russian Federation.

trajectory.title: Youngest Soviet Master
trajectory.description: Became the youngest Soviet master in chess history at age 15 while training under Mikhail Botvinnik's prestigious chess school.

trajectory.title: World Junior Champion
trajectory.description: Won the World Junior Chess Championship in Stockholm with an undefeated 10/11 score, earning the International Master title.

trajectory.title: Grandmaster title
trajectory.description: Earned the international grandmaster title at age 19, becoming the world's youngest grandmaster at the time.

trajectory.title: Candidates Matches winner
trajectory.description: Defeated Polugaevsky, Spassky, and Korchnoi in the Candidates cycle to earn the right to challenge Bobby Fischer for the world title.

trajectory.title: World Chess Champion
trajectory.description: Crowned the 12th World Chess Champion when Fischer refused to defend his title under FIDE conditions.

trajectory.title: First title defense
trajectory.description: Narrowly retained his world title against Viktor Korchnoi in Baguio, Philippines, winning the 32nd and final game.

trajectory.title: Second title defense
trajectory.description: Defeated Korchnoi again in Merano, winning 6-2 to retain the World Championship.

trajectory.title: Lost world title to Kasparov
trajectory.description: Lost the World Championship to Garry Kasparov, ending a decade as world champion and beginning one of chess's greatest rivalries.

trajectory.title: FIDE World Champion
trajectory.description: Recaptured the FIDE World Championship title and successfully defended it in 1996 and 1998.

name: Celine Dion
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Eurovision Song Contest in 1988 at age 20 representing Switzerland, and had already recorded nine French-language albums with numerous Felix and Juno awards by age 18, making her a teen star across the Francophone world.
early_history_summary: The youngest of 14 children in a poor but musical family in Charlemagne, Quebec, Dion began performing at her parents' piano bar at age five. At twelve, she and her mother wrote her first song, and a demo was sent to manager René Angélil, who was so moved he mortgaged his home to fund her debut album in 1981 when she was 13. She released nine French-language albums during the 1980s, won multiple Felix and Juno awards, became the first Canadian artist to receive a gold record in France, and won the Eurovision Song Contest in 1988 at age 20.
family_context_summary: Born the youngest of 14 children to Thérèse (née Tanguay), a homemaker, and Adhémar Dion, a butcher, in Charlemagne, Quebec. The family was poor; Dion wore hand-me-downs, shared a bed with sisters, and slept in a drawer as a baby. Both parents were musical: her mother was a violinist and her father an accordionist, and the family performed together.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were musicians (mother violinist, father accordionist) who ran a small piano bar called Le Vieux Baril. The family formed a singing group called Dion's Family and toured Canada when Céline was an infant. Music was deeply embedded in family life, with most of the 14 children active in show business.
evidence_summary: Dion's early path was defined by an extraordinary vocal gift discovered in a poor but deeply musical family of 14 children in rural Quebec. Her parents were both musicians who ran a piano bar where she performed from age five. At twelve, her mother helped write her first song, and a demo reached manager René Angélil, who mortgaged his home to fund her debut album. Angélil's total commitment as a sustained mentor was the catalytic advantage. By 18 she had nine albums and multiple awards; at 20 she won Eurovision. Despite poverty and bullying, her prodigy-level voice and early immersion in performance drove her rapid ascent.
starting_point: Born in 1968 in Charlemagne, Quebec, the youngest of 14 children in a large, musically inclined working-class family.
current_position: One of the best-selling music artists of all time with over 220 million albums sold worldwide; diagnosed with stiff-person syndrome in 2022, pausing performances.

trajectory.title: First TV appearance and debut album
trajectory.description: Made her Quebec television debut on Michel Jasmin's talk show and released her first album 'La voix du bon Dieu,' financed by manager René Angélil mortgaging his house.

trajectory.title: Yamaha World Popular Song Festival gold
trajectory.description: Won the gold medal at the Yamaha World Popular Song Festival in Tokyo, performing for 115 million TV viewers.

trajectory.title: Eurovision Song Contest winner
trajectory.description: Won the Eurovision Song Contest in Dublin representing Switzerland with 'Ne partez pas sans moi,' before 600 million viewers.

trajectory.title: First English-language album
trajectory.description: Released 'Unison,' her first English-language album, with the single 'Where Does My Heart Beat Now' reaching #4 on the US charts.

trajectory.title: 'Beauty and the Beast' and Grammy
trajectory.description: Recorded the Disney theme song 'Beauty and the Beast' which won the Academy Award and a Grammy Award, cementing her international breakthrough.

trajectory.title: Grammy Album of the Year
trajectory.description: Album 'Falling into You' won Grammy Album of the Year and became one of the best-selling albums of all time.

trajectory.title: 'My Heart Will Go On' and Titanic
trajectory.description: Recorded 'My Heart Will Go On' for the film Titanic, one of the best-selling singles in history; 'Let's Talk About Love' sold over 30 million copies.

trajectory.title: Las Vegas residency
trajectory.description: Began 'A New Day...' residency at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas, running for five years and becoming one of the highest-grossing concert residencies ever.

trajectory.title: 'Courage' album and tour
trajectory.description: Released 'Courage,' her 14th studio album to top the Billboard chart, and embarked on a world tour before health issues intervened.

name: Roger Federer
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first Wimbledon title in 2003 at age 21, and by age 26 (August 2007) had accumulated 12 Grand Slam singles titles including five consecutive Wimbledon championships, reaching world No. 1 in 2004.
early_history_summary: Born in Basel to a Swiss father and South African mother, both employed at Ciba-Geigy Pharmaceuticals, Federer started playing tennis at age three on the company's private courts. He became the best in his age group by six, enrolled in the elite junior program at Old Boys Tennis Club at eight, and was coached by Peter Carter from ages 10 to 14 and 16 to 19. He won the U12 Swiss national junior championship at 12, trained at the Swiss National Tennis Center in Ecublens from 14, won the Wimbledon junior singles and doubles titles in 1998 at 17, and was named ITF World Junior Champion. He won his first ATP title in 2001 at 19 and his first Wimbledon in 2003 at 21.
family_context_summary: Born in Basel to Robert Federer, a Swiss father from Berneck, and Lynette Federer (née Durand), an Afrikaner mother from Kempton Park, South Africa. Both parents worked for Ciba-Geigy Pharmaceuticals, providing a middle-class background. He has one older sister, Diana. The family had access to the company's private tennis courts where Federer first played at age three.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were not tennis professionals but worked at Ciba-Geigy, whose private tennis courts provided Federer's earliest playing environment. His mother enrolled him in the elite junior program at Old Boys Tennis Club at age eight, showing active investment in his tennis development. No evidence of parental tennis expertise or professional sports background.
evidence_summary: Federer's early path was shaped by the Swiss tennis development pipeline: company tennis courts at Ciba-Geigy where his parents worked, elite junior training at Old Boys Tennis Club from age eight, and the Swiss National Tennis Center at Ecublens from age 14. His most influential coach, Peter Carter, provided sustained individualized coaching from ages 10 to 19, credited by Federer for his entire technique. He won the Wimbledon junior title at 17 and was ITF World Junior Champion in 1998. His parents' middle-class stability and access to company tennis courts provided early infrastructure. A difficult period at Ecublens, dealing with bullying and homesickness, fostered his independence. By 21 he won his first Wimbledon, and by 26 he had 12 Grand Slam titles.
starting_point: Born in 1982 in Basel, Switzerland, to a Swiss-German father and South African mother; grew up in a middle-class suburban family.
current_position: Retired professional tennis player; won 20 Grand Slam singles titles and held world No. 1 for 310 weeks; co-founder of the Laver Cup and active philanthropist through the Roger Federer Foundation.

trajectory.title: ATP debut
trajectory.description: Made his ATP tournament debut at age 17, beginning a 24-year professional career.

trajectory.title: Defeated Sampras at Wimbledon
trajectory.description: Upset seven-time Wimbledon champion Pete Sampras in the fourth round at Centre Court, announcing his arrival on the world stage.

trajectory.title: First Wimbledon title
trajectory.description: Won his first Grand Slam singles title at Wimbledon, defeating Mark Philippoussis in the final.

trajectory.title: World No. 1 and 3 Grand Slams
trajectory.description: Became world No. 1 for the first time, winning three Grand Slam titles (Australian Open, Wimbledon, US Open) and beginning a record 237-week reign at No. 1.

trajectory.title: Career Grand Slam completed
trajectory.description: Won his first French Open to complete the Career Grand Slam, then won a 15th major at Wimbledon, surpassing Sampras's all-time record.

trajectory.title: 7th Wimbledon and Olympic silver
trajectory.description: Won his 7th Wimbledon title, returned to world No. 1, and won Olympic silver in singles at the London Olympics.

trajectory.title: Comeback Australian Open
trajectory.description: Won the Australian Open after a six-month injury layoff, his 18th major, defeating Rafael Nadal in a five-set final.

trajectory.title: 20th and final Grand Slam
trajectory.description: Won his 6th Australian Open title, becoming the first man to reach 20 Grand Slam singles titles.

trajectory.title: Retirement
trajectory.description: Announced his retirement from professional tennis, playing his final match at the Laver Cup in London.

name: Cristiano Ronaldo
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 2007-08 UEFA Champions League with Manchester United and was awarded his first Ballon d'Or at age 23 in December 2008, having already won three Premier League titles and the 2008 FIFA Club World Cup.
early_history_summary: Born in a working-class family in Madeira, Ronaldo began playing for Andorinha at age 7, moved to Nacional at 10, and was signed by Sporting CP's academy at 12, relocating alone to Lisbon. He made his first-team debut for Sporting at 17, was signed by Manchester United at 18 after impressing Alex Ferguson in a friendly, and rapidly developed into one of the world's best players, winning the Ballon d'Or at 23.
family_context_summary: Born to a municipal gardener father who was also a part-time kit man at a local football club, and a mother who worked as a cook and cleaner. The family was working-class in one of Madeira's poorest neighborhoods. His father struggled with alcoholism after serving in the Portuguese Colonial War, and died when Ronaldo was 20. Ronaldo was the youngest of four children.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father's role as kit man at Andorinha provided direct early exposure to football, and his godfather was a player at the club who facilitated his introduction. The family had no financial resources but football was woven into daily life through his father's involvement.
evidence_summary: Ronaldo grew up in poverty in Madeira with a father who worked as a kit man at the local football club, giving him direct early exposure to the sport. Recognized as a phenom by age 10, he was signed by Sporting CP's academy at 12 and moved alone to Lisbon, demonstrating exceptional dedication. The Sporting CP academy pipeline and subsequent signing by Manchester United under Alex Ferguson provided elite institutional support. His combination of prodigy-level physical talent, extreme early specialization, and the Portuguese football development system enabled him to win the Ballon d'Or by 23 despite having no financial resources.
starting_point: Born in 1984 in Funchal, Madeira, Portugal, into a working-class family; father was a municipal gardener and part-time kit man.
current_position: Plays for and captains Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia and the Portugal national team; all-time top international goalscorer with 146 goals; five-time Ballon d'Or winner.

trajectory.title: Professional debut at Sporting CP
trajectory.description: Made his first-team debut for Sporting CP, scoring four goals in his first 28 appearances and winning the Portuguese Super Cup.

trajectory.title: Signed by Manchester United
trajectory.description: Joined Manchester United for €19 million after impressing Alex Ferguson in a pre-season friendly, becoming the first Portuguese player at the club.

trajectory.title: Champions League and first Ballon d'Or
trajectory.description: Won the UEFA Champions League with Manchester United and was awarded his first Ballon d'Or and FIFA World Player of the Year.

trajectory.title: Record transfer to Real Madrid
trajectory.description: Transferred to Real Madrid for a then-world-record €94 million, beginning a nine-year tenure where he scored 451 goals in 438 appearances.

trajectory.title: Champions League and Euro 2016
trajectory.description: Won the Champions League with Real Madrid and captained Portugal to victory at Euro 2016, the country's first major international trophy.

trajectory.title: Transfer to Juventus
trajectory.description: Joined Juventus for €100 million, winning two Serie A titles in three seasons in Italy.

trajectory.title: Return to Manchester United and international record
trajectory.description: Returned to Manchester United and became the all-time top international goalscorer, surpassing Ali Daei's record of 109 goals.

trajectory.title: Joined Al-Nassr
trajectory.description: Signed with Al-Nassr in the Saudi Pro League after his Manchester United departure, becoming the highest-paid footballer in history.

name: Yo-Yo Ma
milestone_by_age_26: Awarded the Avery Fisher Prize in 1978 (age 23), the most prestigious award for American classical instrumentalists, recognizing him as one of the world's leading cellists. He had already debuted at Carnegie Hall at age 9 and graduated from Harvard in 1976.
early_history_summary: Ma began studying cello with his father at age four in Paris, gave his first public recital at five, and moved to New York at age seven to study at Juilliard with Leonard Rose. He performed at Carnegie Hall at age nine, played at the Marlboro Festival under Pablo Casals, and graduated from Harvard in 1976 before receiving the Avery Fisher Prize in 1978.
family_context_summary: Ma was born to Chinese parents in Paris: his father Hiao-Tsiun Ma was a violinist, composer, and professor of music, and his mother Marina Lu was a singer. The family moved to Boston when Ma was seven and then to New York for his Juilliard studies. His sister Yeou-Cheng also played violin and piano professionally before becoming a pediatrician.
parent_family_domain_summary: Ma's father was a musicologist, violinist, and composer who specialized in the education of gifted children and personally taught Yo-Yo the cello from age four using a custom method. His mother was a singer. This is a direct and exceptionally strong family-domain advantage.
evidence_summary: Yo-Yo Ma's early trajectory was defined by an exceptionally strong family-domain apprenticeship: his father, a musicologist specializing in gifted children's education, taught him cello from age four using a structured method. By five he had performed publicly, by nine he had debuted at Carnegie Hall, and he studied at Juilliard with Leonard Rose from 1964 to 1971. The family relocated from Paris to Boston and then New York to support his training. His prodigy status was confirmed by comparisons to Casals and Rostropovich, culminating in the Avery Fisher Prize at age 23.
starting_point: Born in 1955 in Paris to Chinese parents; father was a violinist and music professor who began teaching Yo-Yo cello at age four.
current_position: One of the most celebrated cellists in history with over 120 albums and 20 Grammy Awards; founder of Silkroad; United Nations Messenger of Peace.

trajectory.title: Performed for US Presidents
trajectory.description: Performed for Presidents Kennedy and Eisenhower at a National Cultural Center benefit concert in Washington, D.C., establishing himself as a child prodigy.

trajectory.title: Graduated from Harvard
trajectory.description: Graduated from Harvard University with a degree in anthropology, having studied cello at Juilliard under Leonard Rose before pursuing liberal arts education.

trajectory.title: Avery Fisher Prize
trajectory.description: Awarded the Avery Fisher Prize, the most prestigious award for American instrumentalists, recognizing his emergence as a leading classical musician.

trajectory.title: First Grammy Award
trajectory.description: Won his first Grammy Award for his recording of Bach's Unaccompanied Cello Suites, which became a landmark classical recording.

trajectory.title: Founded Silkroad Ensemble
trajectory.description: Established the Silkroad Project, a global music collective creating cross-cultural work with artists from diverse traditions, commissioning over 100 new works.

trajectory.title: National Medal of Arts
trajectory.description: Received the National Medal of Arts from President George W. Bush, the highest US government award for artists.

trajectory.title: Presidential Medal of Freedom
trajectory.description: Received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Obama and Kennedy Center Honors in the same year.

trajectory.title: Bach Project launched
trajectory.description: Launched the Bach Project, a 36-community, six-continent tour performing Bach's Cello Suites paired with local cultural programming.

name: Martina Navratilova
milestone_by_age_26: Won Wimbledon singles title in July 1978 at age 21 and became world No. 1, having already won her first professional singles title at 17 (1974), reached two Grand Slam singles finals at 18 (1975), and won Grand Slam doubles titles.
early_history_summary: Navratilova started playing tennis at age 4, won the Czechoslovak national championship at 15, and her first professional singles title at 17. After defecting from communist Czechoslovakia at 18 in 1975, she reached two Grand Slam singles finals that year. She won her first Wimbledon singles title in 1978 at 21 and became world No. 1.
family_context_summary: Born Martina Šubertová in Prague. Parents divorced when she was 3. Mother Jana was an accomplished gymnast, tennis player, and ski instructor. Stepfather Miroslav Navrátil became her first tennis coach. Grandmother Agnes Semanska was a tennis player ranked No. 2 in Czechoslovakia.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother was an accomplished gymnast, tennis player, and ski instructor. Stepfather was her first tennis coach. Grandmother was a nationally ranked Czechoslovak tennis player (No. 2). Deep family tennis lineage.
evidence_summary: Navratilova was born into a family with deep tennis roots: her grandmother was a nationally ranked Czechoslovak player, her mother was a multi-sport athlete, and her stepfather became her first tennis coach. She started playing at age 4, won the Czechoslovak national championship at 15, and her first professional title at 17. After defecting from communist Czechoslovakia at 18 in 1975, she reached two Grand Slam singles finals that same year. By 21, she won Wimbledon and became world No. 1. The combination of family tennis lineage, early intensive training, and the urgency of defection catalyzed her extraordinary career.
starting_point: Born in 1957 in Prague, Czechoslovakia; mother was a gymnast and tennis coach, stepfather built her first tennis racket.
current_position: Retired tennis legend with 18 Grand Slam singles titles and a record 9 Wimbledon singles titles; tennis commentator and LGBTQ+ activist.

trajectory.title: Defection to the United States
trajectory.description: Defected from Czechoslovakia during the US Open, seeking political asylum and later becoming a US citizen to pursue her tennis career freely.

trajectory.title: First Wimbledon and world No. 1
trajectory.description: Won her first Wimbledon singles title, defeating Chris Evert in the final, and captured the world No. 1 ranking for the first time.

trajectory.title: Career Grand Slam and 86-1 season
trajectory.description: Completed the Career Grand Slam by winning the US Open and posted an astonishing 86-1 match record for the season, the best winning percentage in tennis history.

trajectory.title: Six consecutive Grand Slams
trajectory.description: Won six consecutive Grand Slam singles titles from Wimbledon 1983 through the US Open 1984, equaling the record set by Maureen Connolly and Margaret Court.

trajectory.title: Sixth consecutive Wimbledon
trajectory.description: Won her sixth consecutive Wimbledon singles title, surpassing Suzanne Lenglen's record of five straight, cementing her grass-court dominance.

trajectory.title: Record 9th Wimbledon
trajectory.description: Won her ninth and final Wimbledon singles title, an all-time record that still stands.

trajectory.title: Retired from singles
trajectory.description: Retired from singles competition with 167 career singles titles, the Open Era record, and 18 Grand Slam singles titles.

trajectory.title: Oldest major title winner
trajectory.description: Won the US Open mixed doubles title with Bob Bryan just before her 50th birthday, becoming the oldest player to win a major championship, 32 years after her first.

name: Nadia Comăneci
milestone_by_age_26: Scored the first perfect 10.0 in Olympic gymnastics history at the 1976 Montreal Games at age 14, winning three Olympic gold medals (all-around, uneven bars, balance beam), a silver, and a bronze. She went on to win World Championship golds in 1978-79 and two more Olympic golds in 1980.
early_history_summary: Comăneci was discovered by Béla Károlyi at age 6 when he spotted her turning cartwheels in a schoolyard in Onești, Romania. She entered her first competition at 7, won the Romanian National Junior Championship at 9, and won three golds at her first international junior meet in 1972. By 1975 she was senior European champion, and at 14 she made Olympic history in Montreal.
primary_leverage_engine: Physical talent and extreme early specialization
family_context_summary: Born to Gheorghe (an auto mechanic) and Ștefania Comăneci in Onești, a small industrial town in the Carpathian Mountains. Her parents separated in the 1970s. The family was working class; Nadia's gymnastics training was funded through the Romanian state sports system.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family connection to gymnastics; Comăneci was discovered by coach Béla Károlyi at age 6 in a schoolyard. Her success was driven by the Romanian state gymnastics pipeline rather than family domain advantage.
evidence_summary: Comăneci was discovered at age 6 by Béla Károlyi, who built an experimental gymnastics school in Onești. She trained intensively (8 hours/day, 6 days/week from age 12) within the Romanian state sports system. Her working-class family had no gymnastics background; her father was an auto mechanic. Károlyi's sustained, individualized coaching from age 6 and the state-funded gymnastics pipeline were the dominant early advantages. Her natural physical talent was evident from the start, and her extraordinary composure at age 14 produced the first perfect 10 in Olympic history.
starting_point: Born in 1962 in Onești, Romania, to an auto mechanic father and homemaker mother; discovered at age six by gymnastics coach Béla Károlyi.
current_position: Retired five-time Olympic gold medalist; lives in the United States, co-owns Bart Conner Gymnastics Academy in Oklahoma with husband Bart Conner; gymnastics commentator and humanitarian.

trajectory.title: European Championships dominance
trajectory.description: Won four gold medals at the European Championships in Skien, Norway, establishing herself as the world's leading gymnast before her Olympic debut.

trajectory.title: First Olympic perfect 10
trajectory.description: Scored the first perfect 10.0 in Olympic gymnastics history at the Montreal Games, earning seven perfect 10s and winning three gold medals including the all-around.

trajectory.title: World Championship balance beam
trajectory.description: Won her only individual World Championship title on the balance beam at the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Strasbourg.

trajectory.title: Two more Olympic golds
trajectory.description: Won two gold medals (balance beam and floor exercise) and two silver medals at the Moscow Olympics, bringing her career total to nine Olympic medals.

trajectory.title: Retirement from competition
trajectory.description: Won the World Student Games and effectively retired from competitive gymnastics as physical development began to inhibit her performance.

trajectory.title: Defection from Romania
trajectory.description: Defected from Communist Romania via Hungary to the United States, shortly before the Romanian Revolution that toppled the Ceaușescu regime.

trajectory.title: Marriage to Bart Conner
trajectory.description: Married American Olympic gold-medal gymnast Bart Conner in Bucharest in a televised ceremony attended by millions in Romania.

trajectory.title: US citizenship
trajectory.description: Became a naturalized citizen of the United States while retaining her Romanian identity and connections.

name: Ayrton Senna
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first Formula One Grand Prix at the 1985 Portuguese GP (age 25), having already won the British and European Formula Ford championships (1981), British F3 Championship and Macau Grand Prix (1983), and debuted in F1 with Toleman in 1984 scoring multiple podiums.
early_history_summary: Senna began competitive kart racing at age 13 in 1973, using a go-kart built by his father. He was twice runner-up at the Karting World Championship (1979, 1980). He moved to England in 1981 to race Formula Ford 1600, winning the British and European championships. He dominated Formula Ford 2000 in 1982, won the British F3 Championship in 1983, and entered F1 with Toleman in 1984 before moving to Lotus in 1985 where he took his first pole and victory.
family_context_summary: Born to a wealthy Brazilian family in São Paulo. His father Milton Guirado da Silva was a landowner and factory owner who operated a metallurgical company (Universal) supplying auto manufacturers, with additional investments in construction, farms, and livestock. Senna was the middle child of three.
parent_family_domain_summary: Senna's father Milton owned a metallurgical company supplying the automotive industry and built Ayrton's first go-kart using a lawnmower engine. The family's wealth funded Ayrton's early karting career and supported his move to European racing, though Milton initially hoped Ayrton would join the family business.
evidence_summary: Senna was born into a wealthy São Paulo family; his father Milton owned a metallurgical company supplying the automotive industry and built Ayrton's first go-kart at age 4. Senna started competitive karting at 13, was twice World Championship runner-up, then dominated British Formula Ford and F3 before entering F1 at 24. His father's wealth funded his early racing career, and the family's automotive business provided direct domain proximity. His natural driving talent was evident from his first kart race, where he started on pole against older drivers.
starting_point: Born in 1960 in São Paulo, Brazil, into a wealthy family; father was a factory owner and landowner who gave him his first go-kart at age four.
current_position: Died on May 1, 1994, at age 34, from a crash during the San Marino Grand Prix at Imola; three-time Formula One World Champion and one of the greatest drivers in motorsport history.

trajectory.title: First kart race
trajectory.description: Raced a kart for the first time and immediately won, beginning a karting career that would lay the foundation for his Formula One future.

trajectory.title: Single-seater racing in Britain
trajectory.description: Moved to England for single-seater racing, winning the Formula Ford 1600 and Formula Ford 2000 championships in successive seasons.

trajectory.title: F1 debut with Toleman
trajectory.description: Made his Formula One debut with Toleman, stunning the paddock with a sensational second place behind Alain Prost in torrential rain at Monaco.

trajectory.title: First Grand Prix victory
trajectory.description: Won his first Formula One Grand Prix at the Portuguese GP in Estoril with Lotus, dominating in wet conditions from pole position.

trajectory.title: First World Championship
trajectory.description: Won his first World Drivers' Championship with McLaren-Honda, taking eight Grand Prix victories in the dominant MP4/4 and beginning his legendary rivalry with Alain Prost.

trajectory.title: Second World Championship
trajectory.description: Won his second World Championship after a controversial collision with Prost at the Suzuka first corner, securing the title by a single point.

trajectory.title: Third World Championship
trajectory.description: Won his third World Championship with seven victories including his first home Brazilian Grand Prix, achieving a lifelong dream.

trajectory.title: Record sixth Monaco victory
trajectory.description: Won his record-breaking sixth Monaco Grand Prix and finished runner-up in the championship in his final season at McLaren before moving to Williams.

trajectory.title: Death at Imola
trajectory.description: Killed in a crash while leading the San Marino Grand Prix at Imola on May 1, 1994, prompting sweeping safety reforms in Formula One.

name: Steffi Graf
milestone_by_age_26: On May 25, 1983 at age 13, Graf became the youngest player in tennis history to win a match in a Grand Slam tournament, defeating Carina Karlsson at the French Open. She won the Olympic tennis demonstration event at age 15 in 1984, reached world No. 6 by 1985, and won her first WTA title at age 16 in April 1986.
early_history_summary: Born in Brühl, West Germany, Graf was introduced to tennis at age 3 by her father Peter Graf, an insurance salesman and car dealer who discovered tennis at 27 and became a regional league player and coach. He owned a tennis hall and devoted himself exclusively to Steffi's training from her early childhood, teaching her with a sawed-off wooden racket in the family living room and at his tennis hall. She won the European Championships in the under-18 category at age 12, turned professional at 13, and became the youngest player to win a Grand Slam match at the 1983 French Open.
family_context_summary: Father Peter Graf was an insurance salesman and car dealer who discovered tennis at 27, became a regional league player, acquired a coaching license, and owned a tennis hall. He introduced Steffi to tennis at age 3 with a sawed-off wooden racket, trained her intensively, and devoted himself exclusively to her career by her early teens. Mother Heidi Graf also supported the family. Peter Graf was known as 'Papa Merciless' for his stern control of almost every aspect of Steffi's life and training.
parent_family_domain_summary: Her father became a tennis coach and owned a tennis hall, providing direct domain expertise, professional facilities, and full-time dedicated coaching from age 3. This is an exceptionally strong family-domain advantage, with the father restructuring his entire career around his daughter's tennis development.
evidence_summary: Graf's early career was defined by an extraordinarily intensive family-domain apprenticeship: her father Peter, a tennis coach who owned a tennis hall, introduced her to the sport at age 3 with a sawed-off wooden racket and devoted himself exclusively to her training. By age 5, a tennis coach described watching her play as 'a moment like this only once in a lifetime.' She won the European under-18 championship at 12, turned pro at 13, and became the youngest Grand Slam match winner in history at the 1983 French Open. The father's tennis hall provided rare early access to professional facilities, and his full-time coaching represented an exceptionally dedicated mentor relationship. Graf's prodigy-level coordination and forehand were evident from early childhood, making her institutional response to her talent unusual from a very young age.
starting_point: Born in 1970 in Mannheim, West Germany, to a car and insurance salesman father who introduced her to tennis at age three and became her primary coach.
current_position: Retired German tennis legend with 22 Grand Slam singles titles and the only Golden Slam in history; married to Andre Agassi; lives in Las Vegas.

trajectory.title: Youngest major main draw player
trajectory.description: Became the youngest player to appear in the main draw of a Grand Slam at the French Open, a record that still stands.

trajectory.title: First WTA title
trajectory.description: Won her maiden WTA singles title at Hilton Head, defeating Chris Evert for the first time and signaling her rise to the top of women's tennis.

trajectory.title: First Grand Slam title
trajectory.description: Won her first Grand Slam singles title at the French Open, defeating Martina Navratilova in three sets and becoming world No. 1 later that year.

trajectory.title: Golden Slam
trajectory.description: Achieved the unprecedented calendar-year Golden Slam, winning all four Grand Slam singles titles and Olympic gold at Seoul, the only player ever to do so.

trajectory.title: Three of four Grand Slams
trajectory.description: Won three of four Grand Slam titles and the WTA Finals, maintaining her world No. 1 ranking throughout the year.

trajectory.title: Return to dominance
trajectory.description: Returned to world No. 1 and won three Grand Slam titles following the stabbing of rival Monica Seles, reclaiming her position as the dominant player in women's tennis.

trajectory.title: Quadruple Career Grand Slam
trajectory.description: Won three of four Grand Slams and became the only player in history to win each of the four major singles titles at least four times.

trajectory.title: 22nd major and retirement
trajectory.description: Won her 22nd and final Grand Slam title at the French Open, reached the Wimbledon final, and retired from professional tennis aged 30, ranked world No. 3.

name: Rafael Nadal
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 2005 French Open at age 19, becoming the youngest male Grand Slam champion since Michael Chang in 1989 and the first man to win Roland Garros on debut since Mats Wilander in 1982.
early_history_summary: Nadal was introduced to tennis at age three by his uncle Toni Nadal, a coach at the Manacor Tennis Club in Mallorca. He won the Spanish junior championship at ages 11-12, the ITF World Junior Championship for U14 at 14, and turned professional at 14 in 2001. By 2004 he helped Spain win the Davis Cup final beating world No. 2 Andy Roddick at 18, and in 2005 won the French Open on his first attempt, compiling a 24-match clay-court winning streak.
family_context_summary: Nadal's father Sebastián is a businessman owning an insurance company, a glass and window company, and a restaurant in Mallorca. His uncle Miguel Ángel Nadal was a professional footballer who played for FC Barcelona and the Spanish national team. His uncle Toni Nadal was a tennis coach who trained him from age three.
parent_family_domain_summary: Uncle Toni Nadal was a tennis coach at the Manacor Tennis Club who introduced Rafael to tennis at age three and coached him through his entire junior and early professional career. Uncle Miguel Ángel was a professional footballer at the highest level, providing elite-athlete family context.
evidence_summary: Nadal's path was shaped by deep family-domain immersion: his uncle Toni, a tennis coach, introduced him to the sport at age three and provided sustained individualized coaching throughout his development. His father, a businessman, covered training costs when the family declined a federation scholarship to Barcelona. Nadal showed prodigious talent early, winning an U-12 regional championship at age eight and the Spanish junior championship by eleven. The combination of family coaching, financial stability, and extraordinary physical talent created one of the most successful teenage tennis careers in ATP history, culminating in the 2005 French Open title at age 19.
starting_point: Born in 1986 in Manacor, Mallorca, Spain, to a businessman father and a mother who was a perfumery owner; uncle Toni Nadal introduced him to tennis at age three.
current_position: Retired professional tennis player; won 22 Grand Slam singles titles including a record 14 French Open titles; announced retirement in October 2024.

trajectory.title: First French Open title
trajectory.description: Won the French Open on his tournament debut, becoming the youngest male Grand Slam champion since Pete Sampras and winning 11 titles in a single season.

trajectory.title: Wimbledon classic and Olympic gold
trajectory.description: Defeated Roger Federer in a legendary five-set Wimbledon final, won Olympic singles gold in Beijing, and became world No. 1 for the first time.

trajectory.title: First Australian Open
trajectory.description: Won his first Australian Open title on hard court, defeating Federer in five sets, and completed the Career Grand Slam on all surfaces.

trajectory.title: Three Grand Slams and Career Grand Slam
trajectory.description: Won the French Open, Wimbledon, and US Open in the same year, completing the Career Grand Slam and becoming the youngest man in the Open Era to do so.

trajectory.title: Comeback and two Grand Slams
trajectory.description: Returned from a seven-month injury layoff to win the French Open and US Open, reclaiming the year-end world No. 1 ranking.

trajectory.title: French Open and US Open
trajectory.description: Won a 10th French Open title ('La Decima') and the US Open, becoming the first man in the Open Era to win 10 titles at a single tournament.

trajectory.title: Two Grand Slams and 22nd major
trajectory.description: Won the Australian Open from two sets down in the final and a 14th French Open, becoming the first man to reach 22 Grand Slam singles titles.

trajectory.title: Retirement
trajectory.description: Announced his retirement from professional tennis in October 2024, playing his final match for Spain in the Davis Cup quarterfinals in Málaga.

name: Boris Becker
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Wimbledon gentlemen's singles title on July 7, 1985 at age 17, becoming the youngest-ever male Grand Slam singles champion and the first unseeded player and first German to win Wimbledon.
early_history_summary: Becker joined TC Blau-Weiß Leimen tennis club in 1974 at age 7 and began training under Boris Breskvar. By 1977, he was on the Baden Tennis Association junior team and was selected for the German Tennis Federation's top junior team by Richard Schönborn, with training funded at over 1.3 million DM. He won the Orange Bowl doubles in 1982, turned professional in 1984 under coaches Günther Bosch and Ion Țiriac, won his first top-level singles title at Queen's Club in June 1985, and two weeks later won Wimbledon at age 17.
family_context_summary: Born in Leimen, West Germany, the son of Elvira and Karl-Heinz Becker, an architect who founded a tennis centre in Leimen where Becker learned to play. His mother was a Sudeten German from Moravia. He was raised Catholic and named after Boris Pasternak.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Karl-Heinz Becker, an architect, founded a tennis centre in Leimen, providing direct access to tennis facilities from childhood. This was a directly catalytic family-domain advantage for a future tennis champion.
evidence_summary: Becker's path to Wimbledon champion at 17 was built on deep early advantages: his father founded the tennis centre where he trained from age 7, the German Tennis Federation invested over 1.3 million DM in his development, and he received sustained coaching from Boris Breskvar and later Günther Bosch and Ion Țiriac. His exceptional physical talent was evident early—he was the youngest-ever male Grand Slam champion. The combination of family-domain proximity (tennis centre), institutional pipeline (Federation funding), and dedicated coaching created an unusually concentrated development environment.
starting_point: Born in 1968 in Leimen, West Germany, to an architect father who built the local tennis center where Becker learned to play.
current_position: Former world No. 1 tennis player with 6 Grand Slam titles; released from UK prison in December 2022 after serving 8 months for bankruptcy fraud; deported to Germany.

trajectory.title: Turned professional
trajectory.description: Turned professional under coach Günther Bosch and manager Ion Țiriac, winning his first professional doubles title in Munich.

trajectory.title: Wimbledon champion
trajectory.description: Won Wimbledon at age 17 years and 7 months, becoming the youngest men's singles champion in history and the first unseeded player to win the title.

trajectory.title: Defended Wimbledon title
trajectory.description: Successfully defended his Wimbledon crown, defeating world No. 1 Ivan Lendl in straight sets in the final.

trajectory.title: Third Wimbledon and US Open doubles gold
trajectory.description: Won his third Wimbledon title with a straight-set victory over Stefan Edberg and won Olympic doubles gold at the Seoul Olympics.

trajectory.title: First Australian Open and world No. 1
trajectory.description: Won his first Australian Open title and ascended to the world No. 1 ranking for the first time in his career.

trajectory.title: Second Australian Open, sixth major
trajectory.description: Won his second Australian Open and sixth and final Grand Slam singles title, capping a career that spanned 49 singles titles.

trajectory.title: Retirement from tennis
trajectory.description: Retired from professional tennis with 49 career singles titles and over $25 million in prize money.

trajectory.title: Coached Novak Djokovic
trajectory.description: Began coaching Novak Djokovic, guiding him to six Grand Slam titles over three years before parting ways in 2016.

trajectory.title: Imprisoned for bankruptcy fraud
trajectory.description: Sentenced to two and a half years in UK prison for hiding assets from bankruptcy trustees; released after eight months and deported to Germany.

name: Garry Kasparov
milestone_by_age_26: Became the youngest undisputed World Chess Champion in history in November 1985 at age 22 by defeating Anatoly Karpov, a record that stood until 2024.
early_history_summary: Born Garik Weinstein in Baku, Azerbaijan SSR, Kasparov began studying chess at age 7 after solving a chess problem his parents had set up. At 10, he entered Mikhail Botvinnik's chess school under coach Vladimir Makogonov. He won the Soviet Junior Championship at 13, the Banja Luka tournament at 16, the World Junior Championship at 17, and became a Grandmaster in 1980 at 17. He became world No. 1 in January 1984 at age 21 and world champion in 1985 at 22.
family_context_summary: Kasparov's father, Kim Moiseyevich Weinstein, was Jewish and died of leukemia when Kasparov was 7. His mother, Klara Shagenovna Kasparova, was Armenian. At 12, he adopted his mother's surname. The family fled anti-Armenian pogroms in Baku in January 1990.
parent_family_domain_summary: His parents set up chess problems that sparked his interest, and his father admired intellectual figures. However, no evidence of professional chess background in the family. His father's early death meant his mother raised him and guided his chess career.
evidence_summary: Kasparov's trajectory was shaped by the Soviet chess pipeline and elite mentoring. From age 10, he trained at Botvinnik's chess school under Makogonov, who developed his positional skills. Botvinnik declared at 11 that 'the future of chess lies in the hands of this young man.' His prodigy-level ability was evident early — Soviet Junior Champion at 13, Grandmaster at 17, world No. 1 at 21. The Soviet state provided the institutional infrastructure, while Botvinnik's school offered sustained, high-level coaching. His father's death at 7 and later fleeing pogroms created adversity but also focus.
starting_point: Born in 1963 in Baku, Azerbaijan SSR, Soviet Union, to a Jewish father and Armenian mother; father died when he was seven, and he took his mother's surname Kasparova.
current_position: Former World Chess Champion living in exile from Russia; chairman of the Human Rights Foundation; author and pro-democracy activist opposing Vladimir Putin.

trajectory.title: Soviet Junior Champion
trajectory.description: Won the Soviet Junior Championship at age 12, repeating the victory the following year and establishing himself as a chess prodigy under trainer Mikhail Botvinnik.

trajectory.title: World under-20 champion
trajectory.description: Won the World Junior Chess Championship at age 17, becoming the youngest winner at the time and earning the grandmaster title.

trajectory.title: First World Championship match
trajectory.description: Challenged Anatoly Karpov for the World Championship in a marathon match that was controversially aborted by FIDE after 48 games with Karpov leading 5-3.

trajectory.title: Youngest World Chess Champion
trajectory.description: Defeated Karpov 13-11 to become the youngest undisputed World Chess Champion in history at age 22, a record he held until 2024.

trajectory.title: Split from FIDE and PCA title
trajectory.description: Broke from FIDE to form the rival Professional Chess Association, defending his world title against Nigel Short under PCA auspices.

trajectory.title: Lost to Deep Blue
trajectory.description: Lost a six-game match to IBM's supercomputer Deep Blue, becoming the first world champion to lose to a computer under standard time controls.

trajectory.title: Lost Classical title to Kramnik
trajectory.description: Lost his Classical World Chess Championship title to Vladimir Kramnik in London, ending 15 years as world champion.

trajectory.title: Retirement from chess
trajectory.description: Retired from competitive chess after 20 years as the world's top-rated player, dedicating himself to Russian pro-democracy activism.

trajectory.title: Chairman of Human Rights Foundation
trajectory.description: Named chairman of the New York-based Human Rights Foundation, succeeding Václav Havel and becoming a leading global voice for democracy and human rights.

name: Novak Djokovic
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first ATP singles title at Amersfoort in July 2006 (age 19), claimed his first Grand Slam title at the 2008 Australian Open (age 20), and by age 26 (2013) had won 6 Grand Slam titles and reached world No. 1.
early_history_summary: Djokovic started playing tennis at age 4 in Kopaonik, Serbia, where his parents ran a pizzeria near three tennis courts. He was identified as a special talent by coach Jelena Gencic at age 6, who trained him for six years. At 13 he moved to Nikola Pilic's academy in Munich. He won the U14 European Championship, claimed his first Futures title at 16, first Challenger title at 17, and broke into the top 100 at 18 before winning his first ATP title at 19.
family_context_summary: Born to Srdjan and Dijana Djokovic in Belgrade. Parents were professional skiers who ran a pizzeria and sports equipment shop in Kopaonik. Family was on a very low budget and took high-interest loans to fund Novak's tennis training. Father made everything subordinate to Novak's development. Two younger brothers also played professional tennis.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were professional skiers and ski instructors, not tennis players. No direct tennis domain expertise was transferred, though the family operated sports-adjacent businesses and recognized athletic talent.
evidence_summary: Djokovic's early career was driven by intense early specialization (tennis from age 4), sustained high-quality mentorship from Jelena Gencic (6 years) and Nikola Pilic, and recognition as a prodigy at age 6. His family made enormous financial sacrifices, taking high-interest loans to fund training. The Yugoslav Wars created severe adversity — embargoes prevented international junior travel, NATO bombings disrupted training, and he practiced in a converted swimming pool. This wartime constraint catalyzed urgency and resilience. His parents' ski background provided no tennis domain expertise, but their athletic orientation and total commitment to Novak's development was a critical enabler.
starting_point: Born in 1987 in Belgrade, Serbia, Yugoslavia, to a pizzeria and skiing resort owner father and a homemaker mother; grew up during the Yugoslav wars and trained at the Niki Pilic Academy in Munich from age 12.
current_position: Professional tennis player with a record 24 Grand Slam singles titles and 428 weeks at world No. 1; won Olympic gold at Paris 2024 to complete the Career Golden Slam.

trajectory.title: Turned professional
trajectory.description: Turned professional at age 16, beginning a career that would make him the most decorated male tennis player in history.

trajectory.title: First ATP title
trajectory.description: Won his first ATP singles title at Amersfoort and claimed his first Masters title in Miami, breaking into the top 20.

trajectory.title: First Grand Slam title
trajectory.description: Won his first Grand Slam title at the Australian Open, ending the Federer-Nadal streak of 11 consecutive majors and announcing the arrival of the 'Big Three' era.

trajectory.title: World No. 1 and three Grand Slams
trajectory.description: Ascended to world No. 1 for the first time, winning three Grand Slam titles, five Masters, and going 10-1 against Federer and Nadal in one of the greatest seasons ever.

trajectory.title: Career Grand Slam completed
trajectory.description: Won the French Open to complete the Career Grand Slam, becoming the first man since Rod Laver in 1969 to hold all four majors simultaneously.

trajectory.title: Longest Wimbledon final
trajectory.description: Won Wimbledon in the longest Grand Slam final in history (4 hours 57 minutes), saving two championship points against Roger Federer.

trajectory.title: Three Grand Slams, one match from calendar Slam
trajectory.description: Won three of four Grand Slam titles, falling one match short of the calendar Grand Slam in the US Open final.

trajectory.title: Record 24th Grand Slam
trajectory.description: Won three Grand Slam titles including a record 10th Australian Open, reaching 24 career majors to stand alone as the all-time men's record holder.

trajectory.title: Olympic gold and Career Golden Slam
trajectory.description: Won Olympic singles gold at the Paris Olympics, completing the Career Golden Slam and becoming the fifth player in history to achieve the feat.

name: Diego Maradona
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1979 FIFA World Youth Championship at age 18, receiving the Golden Ball as tournament best player, and later won the 1986 FIFA World Cup at age 25.
early_history_summary: Maradona was spotted by a talent scout at age 8 and joined the Argentinos Juniors youth team Los Cebollitas. He made his professional debut at age 15 in October 1976, becoming the youngest player in Argentine Primera División history. By 1979, he was the top scorer in Argentine football and led Argentina to the World Youth Championship title.
family_context_summary: Born to a poor family in a shantytown in Villa Fiorito; father worked at a chemicals factory and mother was a homemaker. He was the first son after four daughters.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of parental football expertise or industry connections.
evidence_summary: Maradona's extraordinary football talent was recognized at age 8 when a youth coach could not believe a child could play so well. He joined Argentinos Juniors' youth system and made his professional debut at 15, the youngest in Argentine league history. By 18, he won the World Youth Championship Golden Ball. His family was poor—his father worked in a chemicals factory—and he grew up in a shantytown, but his prodigy-level talent earned him access to elite youth development and dedicated coaching from Francis Cornejo.
starting_point: Born in 1961 in Lanús, Buenos Aires, Argentina, to a factory worker father and a homemaker mother; grew up in a shantytown (villa miseria) as one of eight children.
current_position: Died on November 25, 2020, at age 60, from a heart attack in Dique Luján, Buenos Aires; widely regarded as one of the greatest footballers in history.

trajectory.title: Professional debut
trajectory.description: Made his professional debut for Argentinos Juniors ten days before his 16th birthday, becoming the youngest player ever in Argentina's Primera División.

trajectory.title: FIFA World Youth Championship
trajectory.description: Won the FIFA World Youth Championship with Argentina, receiving the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player.

trajectory.title: Boca Juniors and league title
trajectory.description: Joined Boca Juniors and led the team to the Argentine Primera División title in his single season at the club.

trajectory.title: World record transfer to Barcelona
trajectory.description: Transferred to Barcelona for a then-world-record £5 million and played in his first World Cup, though Argentina was eliminated in the second round.

trajectory.title: World record transfer to Napoli
trajectory.description: Moved to Napoli for a new world-record fee of £6.9 million, where he would achieve the most iconic years of his career.

trajectory.title: World Cup champion
trajectory.description: Captained Argentina to victory at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico, scoring the 'Hand of God' and the 'Goal of the Century' against England in the quarterfinal and winning the Golden Ball.

trajectory.title: Napoli's first Serie A title
trajectory.description: Led Napoli to their first-ever Serie A championship, transforming the club into one of Italy's powerhouses and becoming a deity-like figure in Naples.

trajectory.title: World Cup runner-up and second Serie A
trajectory.description: Led Argentina to the World Cup final (lost to West Germany) and won his second Serie A title with Napoli.

trajectory.title: Drug ban
trajectory.description: Received a 15-month suspension from football after testing positive for cocaine, marking the beginning of his decline from the sport's pinnacle.

trajectory.title: Death
trajectory.description: Died of a heart attack on November 25, 2020, at age 60, prompting three days of national mourning in Argentina and a massive public funeral procession.

name: Usain Bolt
milestone_by_age_26: Won 200m gold at the 2002 World Junior Championships in Kingston at age 15, becoming the youngest ever world junior champion in athletics history; later won Olympic 100m and 200m gold in world record times at the 2008 Beijing Olympics at age 22.
early_history_summary: Born in Sherwood Content, a small rural town in Jamaica, Bolt showed sprinting potential at Waldensia Primary School and was the school's fastest 100m runner by age 12. Coached by Pablo McNeil at William Knibb Memorial High School, he won his first high school medal in 2001 and broke through at the 2002 World Junior Championships in Kingston at age 15, winning 200m gold as the youngest world junior champion ever. He turned professional in 2004 and set the world junior 200m record (19.93s).
family_context_summary: Parents Wellesley and Jennifer Bolt ran the local grocery store in rural Sherwood Content, Jamaica. Working-class background with no athletic or financial platform documented.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no evidence of parental athletic expertise.
evidence_summary: Usain Bolt won 200m gold at the 2002 World Junior Championships at age 15, the youngest world junior champion ever, driven by exceptional physical talent (1.95m tall at 15) and immersion in Jamaica's world-leading sprinting ecosystem. Coached by Pablo McNeil and later supported by the JAAA, he moved from a rural town to Kingston to train. His parents ran a grocery store with no athletic or financial platform. The Jamaican track pipeline and his prodigious physical edge were the dominant early advantages.
starting_point: Born in 1987 in Sherwood Content, Jamaica, to a grocery store owner father and a homemaker mother; grew up in a small rural town in Trelawny Parish.
current_position: Retired Jamaican sprinter and the greatest sprinter of all time; eight-time Olympic gold medalist and world record holder in the 100m (9.58s), 200m (19.19s), and 4x100m relay (36.84s).

trajectory.title: World Junior Championships gold
trajectory.description: Won the 200m at the World Junior Championships in Kingston at age 15, becoming the youngest world junior champion ever in the event.

trajectory.title: Turned professional
trajectory.description: Turned professional and competed at the Athens Olympics, though he failed to advance past the first round in the 200m due to injury.

trajectory.title: Beijing Olympics double and world records
trajectory.description: Won 100m and 200m gold at the Beijing Olympics in world record times (9.69 and 19.30) plus 4x100m relay gold, becoming a global superstar overnight.

trajectory.title: Berlin world records
trajectory.description: Set the current 100m world record of 9.58 seconds and the 200m world record of 19.19 seconds at the World Championships in Berlin, the largest 100m improvement in electronic timing history.

trajectory.title: London Olympics triple gold
trajectory.description: Won the 100m, 200m, and 4x100m relay gold at the London Olympics, becoming the first track athlete to win three Olympic golds at two consecutive Games.

trajectory.title: Rio Olympics 'triple triple'
trajectory.description: Won the sprint triple at the Rio Olympics for a third consecutive Games, achieving the unprecedented 'triple triple' and cementing his status as the greatest sprinter of all time.

trajectory.title: Retirement
trajectory.description: Retired from competitive athletics after the World Championships in London, finishing third in his final individual 100m race and pulling up injured in the relay.
